extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, copyholders, and typesetters preparing/manuscripts and proofs for publication
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing manuscripts, setting tables and type, and performing proofreading/copyholding for book/article publication; includes typographic standards for tables, spacing, headings, proofs, and manuscript handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caps and small caps in table heads and stubs
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever small caps are used in box-heads, the 'stub' (i.e., first column) head should, as a rule, also be set in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caps and small caps consistently between box-heads and stubs so that headings match visually; follow the same type for the body of the table when setting 'Table I' etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing in ruled tables near rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between the horizontal rules and the matter inclosed, and, if practicable, at least the equivalent of an en-quad between the perpendicular rules and the matter inclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear gap (minimum two leads) between horizontal rules and content; give perpendicular rules an en-quad equivalent if practicable to avoid crowding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of periods or leaders in open tables; leaders in stubs
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods, one em apart and aligned, or leaders, may be used between the columns. In ruled tables, in the 'stub,' leaders should usually be employed, if there is room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For open tables use aligned period columns or leaders to guide the eye; in ruled tables prefer leaders in the stub to link row labels to figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader width and alignment in figure columns
rubrics_metrics.description: In columns of figures, to express a blank use leaders the width of the largest number in the column; center the figures in the column; if they cannot be put in the exact center and there is an unequal number of digits in the groups, leave more space on the left than on the right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose leader width based on the widest numeral (e.g., 2-em for four digits); center numerals, and when centering is imperfect prefer slightly more left padding for uneven digit groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centering and hanging indention for reading-matter in columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading-matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered, if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention, and align all on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center column text when possible; if a line wraps, apply hanging indent and left-align wrapped lines to maintain readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules at top of tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables, but perpendicularly, as a usual thing, only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always place a double horizontal rule at the top; use vertical double rules sparingly — typically only for doubled-up tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open vs ruled table rule by column count
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables of two columns only should be set as open; of three or more, as ruled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide table style by column count: two-column tables → open style; three-or-more columns → ruled style with vertical rules and appropriate spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting of table numbers and headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: "Table I," etc., in headlines of tables should ordinarily be set in caps of the type in which the body of the table is set; the following (descriptive) line, if any, in caps and small caps of the same type. A single (descriptive) headline, not preceded by the number of the table, should be set in caps of the type in which the table is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set numeric table label in same-case as the table body; descriptive lines in caps + small caps; unnumbered descriptive headlines in caps matching table type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point and pica measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures. The standard of measurement is the pica. A pica is twelve points (one-sixth of an inch). (Lists sizes and specimen lines set in named point sizes.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the point/pica system to specify sizes; refer to named sizes (pica, small pica, long primer, bourgeois, etc.) when defining type size for consistent composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type styles and manuscript indications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary type is called roman; type with a sloping face is called italic; type with a heavy black face is called bold-face. Italic is indicated in manuscripts by a straight line under the word(s); bold-face by a wavy line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors should mark intended type styles clearly in manuscripts with standard indicators: straight underline for italics, wavy for bold, etc., to prevent compositor errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font components and marking caps/small caps
rubrics_metrics.description: A font includes large capitals (caps), small capitals (small caps), and lower-case letters. Caps are indicated by three straight lines; small caps by two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark manuscript type requests using the indicated proofreader symbols so compositor can select caps/small caps correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard spacing between words and after punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard line should have a 3-em space between all words not separated by other punctuation points than commas, and after commas; an en-quad after semicolons, and colons followed by a lower-case letter; two 3-em spaces after colons followed by a capital; an em-quad after periods, and exclamation and interrogation points, concluding a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these specific space widths after punctuation to preserve typographic conventions and balanced text color; use em/en/quads consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order for adjusting spacing to reduce/increase line length
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary to reduce spacing in a line, begin with commas, and letters of slanting form—i.e., with a large 'shoulder' on the side adjoining the space; if necessary to increase, begin with overlapping letters—i.e., with 'kerns' protruding on the side adjoining the space—straight-up-and-down letters, and points other than periods and commas (in this order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fine-tuning justification, adjust spaces adjacent to slanted letters and punctuation first for least-visible change; when widening, start with kerned/overlapping letters to minimize visual disruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion rule for well-spaced lines and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: In a well-spaced line, with a 3-em space between a majority of the words, there should not be more than an en-quad between the rest; this proportion should be maintained in increasing or reducing. To justify a line is to adjust it, making it even or true, by proper spacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the 3-em majority / en-quad minority spacing balance when justifying lines for even typographic color.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid abrupt spacing contrasts and hair-spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow an exceptionally thin-spaced line with an exceptionally wide-spaced one, or vice versa, if at all avoidable. Never hair-space, or em-quad, a line to avoid a run-over.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid visual 'rivers' or abrupt spacing shifts; do not use hair-spacing/em-quadting as shortcuts to fix run-overs — reflow or reword instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not space out last line of paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not space out the last line of a paragraph allowing of an indention of an em or more at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the terminal line of a paragraph does not have excessive expanded spacing leaving a large end gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around short words
rubrics_metrics.description: Short words, like 'a,' 'an,' etc., should have the same space on each side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep symmetric spacing around short words to avoid visual imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thin space use after special signs and before abbreviations/metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a thin space after §, ^, and similar signs; before 'f.,' 'ff.,' and the metric symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply thin spacing around legal/section symbols and certain bibliographic/metric abbreviations for correct typography and legibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency symbol spacing
rubrics_metrics.description: In American and English sums of money no space is used between the symbols, $ and £ (pounds), s. (shillings), and d. (pence), and the numerals: $2.75; £10 3s. 2d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not insert a space between monetary symbols and numerals in Anglo-American conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing after numerals in heads and headings
rubrics_metrics.description: After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of lines, denoting subsections, there should be an en-quad. After Arabic and Roman numerals at the beginning of center-heads there should be an em-quad. Small-cap headings should have an en-quad between the words; cap-and-small-cap and cap headings, two 3-em spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use en-quad/em-quad and 3-em spacing rules to differentiate numeric headings/subheads and heading case styles for consistent layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scripture reference spacing convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Scripture references should be spaced thus: II Cor. 1:16-20; 2:5—3:12.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this compact spacing style for biblical citations (no extra spaces within chapter:verse ranges and use proper punctuation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing around variables, superscripts, subscripts in formulae
rubrics_metrics.description: Between letters forming products, and before superior figures or letters indicating powers, and inferior figures or letters, ordinarily no space should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In algebraic and scientific formulae avoid spacing between multiplicative letters and adjacent superscripts/subscripts for standard mathematical typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indentation rules by measure and type size
rubrics_metrics.description: In measures of less than 10 picas' width, indent all sizes 1 em. In measures of from 10 to 20, indent ii-pt., 1 em; lo-pt., 1 1/6; 9-pt., 1 1/8; 8-pt., 1 1/12; 6-pt., 2. In measures of 20–30, other specified indents apply. For hanging indentions different specific em values are prescribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the detailed indentation table tied to measure (picas) and type size for consistent paragraph starts and hanging indents — follow the numeric table as given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry setting and indentation by longest line and rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: In poetry, center the longest line and let the indention be governed by that; where consecutive lines rhyme, they should, as a rule, be aligned; if rhymes alternate indent the rhyming lines alike (usually one em), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center poetry by longest line; align lines according to rhyme schemes and length; for blank verse align approximately equal lines; if lines are disproportionately short indent more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer plain paragraphs; use hanging indention selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter 'plain paragraphs' are always preferable. Where it is desired to bring into relief the opening word(s) of a paragraph, or the number introducing such paragraph, or where a center-head makes more than three lines, 'hanging indention' is often employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default to plain paragraphs; reserve hanging indents for emphasis or long center-heads; follow guidelines for when hanging indention is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead and slug standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead is a strip of metal used to separate lines; the ordinary (standard) lead is 2 points thick. A slug is thicker than a lead; standard sizes are 6 and 12 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify leads (2-pt) and slugs (6- or 12-pt) when setting matter to ensure consistent vertical spacing; refer to 'leaded' vs 'solid' type descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running-head sizing and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A running-head is placed at the top of each page, usually giving the main title on the verso and the chapter title on the recto. A good working rule is to set them in roman or italic capitals two sizes (points) smaller than the type of the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set running heads smaller than body type (two points smaller) and follow left/right distribution (main title on verso, chapter on recto) for conventional running-head layout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and handling of proof types
rubrics_metrics.description: Galley-proof: impression in long shallow galley; page-proof: impression made up into page-form; plate- or foundry-proof: proof taken immediately before electrotype cast with black border; foul proof: galley-proof containing author's corrections; revise: new proof corrected from a marked proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know each proof type and when to supply/expect them; foul proofs indicate author's marks and need special handling; plate corrections are expensive and should be avoided if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make-up and folio conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Make-up is arranging type-lines into page-form. A folio is a page-number; even numbers on verso, odd on recto. A drop-folio is a page-number placed at the bottom of a page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow folio placement conventions; ensure make-up follows pagination and folio norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript physical preparation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be either typewritten or in perfectly clear handwriting (typewritten preferable). Sheets should be of uniform size (9"x11" desirable). Only one side of the paper should be used. Never roll manuscripts; place them flat in a box or envelope. Sheets should not be fastened together except by pins or clips. When one piece of a page is to be fastened to another, use mucilage, not pins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must prepare manuscripts to facilitate typesetting: single-sided, uniform sheets, flat storage, removable fastenings, and use adhesive (mucilage) when attaching slips to avoid lost pins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margins, pagination, and inserts marking
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberal margins should be left at the top and left-hand side for reader/printer directions. Pages should be numbered consecutively. Inserted and omitted pages should be clearly indicated (e.g., sheets to be inserted after p. 4 marked '4A','4B'; sheets omitted between p. 4 and p. 8 indicated by numbering p. 4, '4-7'). Additions to original pages placed after the sheets to which they belong and marked 'Insert A', 'Insert B', etc., with 'Here insert A' on the margin of original pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide wide top/left margins and clear pagination/insertion markers so printers can insert/omit pages without error; follow the exact insertion labeling scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph marking in manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraphs should be plainly indicated, either by indenting the first line or by a ^ mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark paragraph breaks clearly in manuscript to avoid mis-setting paragraphs during typesetting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote designation and numbering rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes should be clearly designated, either by separating them from the text by running a line across the page, or by using ink of a different color. The word in the text carrying the note should be followed by a superior figure corresponding to that preceding the note. Footnotes should never be run into the text in manuscripts. Number them consecutively throughout an article or by chapters in a book (because linotype resetting requires this).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate footnotes visibly and use consecutive numbering across the article or by chapter to avoid linotype resetting difficulties; avoid in-text footnote insertion in manuscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with linotype resetting and footnote renumbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that in matter set on the linotype machine the slightest change necessitates the resetting of the whole line. Number footnotes consecutively throughout an article or by chapters; bear in mind that the change, by omission or addition, of one single number involves resetting of the whole first line of each succeeding note to the end of the series, as well as the line in the text bearing the reference to the note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize renumbering or reordering of footnotes once set on linotype; prefer galley-stage corrections and plan numbering to avoid large rework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful handwriting of proper names, foreign words, and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper names, foreign words, and figures should, in handwritten manuscript, be written with the utmost care and distinctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must ensure clarity of names/foreign terms/numerals to prevent compositor errors; unclear items should be clarified or queried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission of copy for front/back matter and indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy for title-pages, prefaces, tables of contents, etc., should be submitted with the manuscript. Copy for indexes should be compiled from the special set of page-proofs furnished for this purpose, and promptly delivered to the printers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide ancillary copy (title-pages, prefaces, TOC) along with manuscript; prepare index copy from supplied page-proofs and deliver promptly to avoid delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading and returning proofs; proof correction economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and return your proofs promptly. In marking proof-sheets, use the standard proofreaders' marks. Be careful to answer all queries in the proofs. Remember that changes in the type cost money; make your manuscript as perfect as possible before delivering it to the printer. Any necessary alterations should be made in the galley-proof, as each succeeding stage will add to the cost. Corrections in plates should be studiously avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond to proof queries quickly, use standard marks, minimize alterations after page-proof to avoid costly resetting and plate corrections; prefer corrections at galley stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Return of original manuscript with proofs and accompanying marked sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The original manuscript should in each instance be returned with the galley-proof, in order that the proofreader may refer to it; and each successive set of proofs returned should be accompanied by the previous marked set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include the original manuscript with the galley and keep a chain of marked proof sets to enable cost accounting and error resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading professional responsibilities and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Read everything as if you yourself were the author. Be particularly careful about proper names and figures. If the copy is not perfectly clear, or if you have reason to doubt its correctness, look it up, or query it to the author. Do not follow copy blindly; follow copy only when, and as far as, it is correct. Do not ask authors or editors to decide questions of style. The Manual of Style is primarily meant for you. Learn its rules so that you may correct any violation of them you may come upon, without asking questions. Do not permit yourself to be stampeded. Cultivate speed, but remember that accuracy is even more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreaders should act as the arbiter of correctness, use judgment when querying authors, prioritize accuracy over speed, and learn the manual to resolve style questions without deferring to authors/editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling pressure and accountability for proofreaders
rubrics_metrics.description: In unavoidable cases of 'rush,' where conditions and orders are imperative, protect yourself by letting it be understood that you have done your best in the time allotted you, but that you must disclaim any further responsibility. Put your initial at the top of every galley you read or revise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working under rush conditions, document limitations/responsibility and initial galleys to record accountability and work performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyholder performance guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a low, soft, clear reading-voice. Remember that small words are as essential as big ones. Enunciate plural 's' distinctly. Regulate and equalize your speed; do not race through typewritten copy. Do not keep guessing at a word. Sit at right angles to your reader if possible. Give your reader a chance to make corrections. Evolve your own system of signals. Do not waste time over matters of style; the proofreader is supposed to know the rules. Be careful in transferring marks. In sending out proofs, see that everything is there. Arrange the copy and proof-sheets neatly and consecutively. Never send out proofs, for the first time, without consulting the job ticket for the number wanted, and the name and address of the person to whom they are to be sent. The manuscript should accompany the galley-proof; the foul proof should accompany the page-proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copyholders should read clearly and steadily, avoid guessing, use compact signal systems, avoid style judgments, transfer marks accurately, ensure completeness before sending proofs, and include manuscripts/foul proofs as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Envelope and file housekeeping for copyroom staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate in the lower left-hand corner the contents of all the envelopes you address. Fasten your pins in the center at the top, not diagonally in the left-hand corner. Return every evening to the file or the bookcase any volume taken out for reference. Keep records, files, etc., orderly so everything can be located quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain neat filing and envelope labeling habits, pin pages at the top center, and return references daily to preserve proofroom organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and meanings of standard proofreader's marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of proofreader's marks and their meanings (examples include: Put in SMALL CAPITALS; Put in lower case; Put in italics; Put in bold face; Delete; Letter reversed — turn; Indent/make a new paragraph; Put in space; Close up — no space; Bad spacing — space more evenly; Wrong font; Transpose; Carry to the left/right; Elevate/Depress; Perfect letter — correct; Space shows between words — shove down; Straighten crooked line; Restore or retain words crossed out; Print as a logotype; Words are omitted from or in copy; Query to author: 'Is this right?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standardized set of marks when correcting proofs so compositors can apply changes unambiguously; see the full symbol list for exact mark-to-action mappings.
